new_statements.quote: The structure of the Bette language as it migrated from the Bantu has not changed. After a careful analysis of the grammatical features of the language it is observed that Bette is highly idiomatic, metaphorical and tonal. It is this tonal variation that gives the language its creative flair (Ashipu,2005).
new_statements.citation: Ashipu, K. B. C. 2015. An analysis of phonostylistic devices in some selected Itiang (proverbs) Bette. Journal of Literature, Languages and Linguistics (IISTE) 11: 1-7.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (7 pp., text, IISTE JLLL vol. 11, 2015). The quoted passage is verbatim on p. 1, Introduction, second paragraph (extracted text): "The structure of the Bette language as it migrated from the Bantu has not changed. After a careful analysis of the grammatical features of the language it is observed that Bette is highly idiomatic, metaphorical and tonal. It is this tonal variation that gives the language its creative flair (Ashipu,2005)." Read the whole paper: it is a literary-stylistics analysis of proverbs (alliteration, ideophones, onomatopoeia); the only other prosodic language is a general Halliday (2004) quotation on p. 3 about melody and "moments of prominence" in speech at large…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule available: the only accessible first-hand remark says Bette is a tone language and says nothing about word stress. All wordlist data (Blench 2010, Aboh et al. 2024 names) are tone-marked, consistent with a tonal language, but no source I could open discusses stress, accent or prominence.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned by any accessible source.
new_statements.domain_note: The tonal remark is a passing characterisation in a literary-stylistics paper by a native-speaker scholar (Dept. of English, University of Calabar), not a phonological description; domain unspecified.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources concern Bette of Obudu LGA (Bette-Obudu) and Bette-Bendi of Obanliku LGA together, i.e. bete1262 proper; Blench 2010 lists 'Bete' and 'Bendi' as separate lects of the same cluster (Ethnologue dialects Bendi and Bete). Not to be confused with Bete of Taraba (byf) or Bété of Côte d'Ivoire (bet), as Offiong 2022 explicitly warns.

sources.citation: Ashipu, K. B. C. 2015. An analysis of phonostylistic devices in some selected Itiang (proverbs) Bette. Journal of Literature, Languages and Linguistics (IISTE) 11: 1-7.
sources.quote: The structure of the Bette language as it migrated from the Bantu has not changed. After a careful analysis of the grammatical features of the language it is observed that Bette is highly idiomatic, metaphorical and tonal. It is this tonal variation that gives the language its creative flair (Ashipu,2005).
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Introduction (p.1) says Bette is 'highly idiomatic, metaphorical and tonal' and that 'tonal variation' gives the language its creative flair; a literary-stylistics paper, no phonological description.

sources.citation: Aboh, Romanus, Angela Ajimase & Idom T. Inyabri. 2024. They do not eat a wife's beauty: the ethnopragmatics of Bette proverbial personal names. Languages 9(9): 302. doi:10.3390/languages9090302
sources.note: Nothing on stress or tone (names are printed with acute/grave accents, i.e. tone-marked, but no phonological statement). Cites Ushie & Imbua 2011 as the reference work on Bendi/Bette.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. 2024. An overview of the Bantoid languages. Afrika und Übersee 97. doi:10.15460/auue.2024.97.1.288
sources.note: No stress statement for any Bantoid group. Tone table (p.23) gives the Bendi row from Bekwara only: 'H, M, L, four glide tones (Stanford 1967)'; nothing on Bette.

sources.citation: Ashipu, K. B. C. 2010. A socio-stylistic analysis of some selected Bette dirges. Lwati: A Journal of Contemporary Research 7(2): 113-124. doi:10.4314/lwati.v7i2.57538
sources.note: Nothing on word stress or tone; only says the language is of 'Bantu stock', a 'sub-group of the Ekoi', and that its orthography is not standardized; talks about rhythm/beats in dirge performance only.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. 2010 [2001]. The Bendi languages: more lost Bantu languages? Draft circulated for comment, 22 Nov 2010, 26 pp. (Comparative)
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Comparative wordlists (Bete forms tone-marked, e.g. ù-ndì / bɛ̀- 'person', ù-ʃǐ 'snake'); Table 2 lists the Bete sources (Bendi mss; Thomas 1914; Williamson ms.) and p.1 mentions 'Ibadan University long essays on Bete by Briggs and Oni' as cited by Faraclas 1989:378. Section 2.3 only says data are transcribed from sources without alteration.

sources.citation: Wikipedia 'Bete-Bendi language', 'Bendi languages', 'Bette people'; Wiktionary 'Appendix:Bendi word lists' (from Blench 2001); Blench's Bendi materials page (rogerblench.info, Internet Archive copy)
sources.note: Nothing on phonology; the Blench page lists only Comparative Bendi, an Obe (Utugwang) cluster survey and wordlists, a Bekwarra grammar and a Bokyi wordlist — no Bette-specific document.
